title: Coral Bleaching and How Reefs Recover
summary: Why corals turn white when the sea stays too warm, what happens to a bleached coral, and how reefs, fish, and people in places like Saudi Arabia help coral recover.
poll: Coral reefs can be saved if people act now.

versions.title: When Coral Turns White
versions.text:
Look at a reef. It looks like rock. But a coral is an animal! It is small and soft. It builds a hard shell. Lots of these shells make a reef.

Small plants live in the coral. They are algae. They use the sun to make food. They share the food. They give the reef its bright hues. They get a safe home.

Now and then, the sea gets too hot. It stays hot for weeks. Then the coral spits out the algae. Now you can see its white shell. This is called bleaching.

A white coral is not dead yet. But it is weak. If the heat stays, it can die. Then weeds grow on it.

But the sea may cool in time. Then the algae can come back. The color comes back. It can recover.

A reef can recover, too. New young ones drift in. They stick to clean rock. Fish eat the weeds. It takes ten years or more.

The Red Sea has some tough ones. They can take more heat. In Saudi Arabia, they grow bits of coral. Then they plant them on reefs.

You can help. Do not touch a reef. Keep the sea clean.

We can help by keeping the sea clean and never touching coral.

versions.title: Coral Bleaching and How Reefs Recover
versions.text:
A coral reef looks like an underwater garden of colorful rocks, but corals are neither rocks nor plants. They are tiny animals called polyps, and each polyp has a soft body and builds a hard skeleton around itself. Over hundreds of years, these skeletons pile up to form an enormous reef that shelters a remarkable variety of fish and other sea creatures.

Inside each polyp live microscopic plant-like organisms called algae. The algae use sunlight to produce food, and they share most of it with the coral. They also give the coral its brilliant colors, while the coral provides the algae with a protected place to live.

Sometimes the temperature of the sea rises too high. If the water remains a degree or two warmer than usual for several weeks, the stressed coral pushes the algae out of its body. Without them, the polyp's soft tissue is nearly transparent, so the white skeleton shows through, and scientists call this process bleaching.

A bleached coral is not dead yet, but it is starving and weak. If the heat continues for too long, the coral can die, and seaweed quickly spreads over its skeleton. If the water cools down in time, however, the algae can return, and the coral gradually regains its color and can recover.

A damaged reef can recover as well. Baby corals drift in and settle on clean rock, while fish such as parrotfish graze on the seaweed that would otherwise smother them. Even so, it can take ten years or more for a reef to grow back.

Some corals in the Red Sea can tolerate more heat than most, so scientists study them closely. In Saudi Arabia, researchers also grow small pieces of coral in underwater nurseries and then plant them on damaged reefs.

People can help by keeping the ocean clean, protecting the fish that care for reefs, and never touching or standing on coral.

versions.title: Coral Bleaching and How Reefs Recover
versions.text:
A coral reef looks like an underwater garden of colorful rocks, but corals are neither rocks nor plants. They are tiny animals called polyps, and each polyp has a soft body and builds a hard skeleton of limestone around itself. Over hundreds of years, these skeletons pile up to form an enormous reef, and although reefs cover only a tiny part of the ocean floor, they shelter about a quarter of all ocean species.

Inside each polyp live microscopic plant-like organisms called algae. The partnership is symbiotic, which means that both partners benefit: the algae use sunlight to produce food and share most of it with the coral, while the coral provides the algae with a protected place to live. The algae also give the coral its brilliant colors.

Sometimes the temperature of the sea rises too high. If the water remains a degree or two warmer than usual for several weeks, the algae begin to produce harmful substances, and the stressed coral pushes them out of its body. Without them, the polyp's soft tissue is nearly transparent, so the white skeleton shows through, and scientists call this process bleaching.

A bleached coral is not dead yet, but it is starving and weak. If the heat continues for too long, the coral can die, and seaweed quickly spreads over its skeleton. If the water cools down in time, however, the algae can return, and the coral gradually regains its color.

A damaged reef can recover as well. Coral larvae, the tiny swimming young of corals, drift in and settle on clean rock, while fish such as parrotfish graze on the seaweed that would otherwise smother them. Even so, it can take ten years or more for a reef to grow back.

Because the oceans are getting warmer, bleaching is happening more often, and the global event that began in 2023 became the largest ever recorded.

Some corals in the Red Sea are unusually resilient to heat, so scientists study them closely. In Saudi Arabia, researchers also grow small pieces of coral in underwater nurseries and then plant them on damaged reefs.

People can help by keeping the ocean clean, protecting the fish that care for reefs, and never touching or standing on coral.

Because the oceans are getting warmer, bleaching is happening more frequently, and the global event that began in 2023 became the most widespread ever recorded.

Some corals in the Red Sea are unusually resilient to heat, so scientists study them closely in order to understand how they survive. In Saudi Arabia, researchers also cultivate small pieces of coral in underwater nurseries and then transplant them onto damaged reefs.

People can help by keeping the ocean clean, protecting the fish that care for reefs, and never touching or standing on coral.

versions.title: Coral Bleaching and How Reefs Recover
versions.text:
A coral reef resembles an underwater garden of colorful rocks, but corals are neither rocks nor plants; they are tiny animals called polyps, and each polyp has a soft body and constructs a hard skeleton of limestone around itself. Over hundreds of years, these skeletons accumulate to form an enormous reef, and although reefs occupy only a tiny fraction of the ocean floor, they shelter approximately a quarter of all marine species.

Inside each polyp live microscopic plant-like organisms called algae. The partnership is symbiotic, which means that both partners benefit: the algae use sunlight to manufacture food and share most of it with the coral, while the coral provides the algae with a protected environment. The algae are also responsible for the coral's brilliant colors.

Sometimes the temperature of the sea rises excessively. If the water remains a degree or two warmer than usual for several weeks, the algae begin to produce harmful substances, and the stressed coral expels them from its body; because the polyp's soft tissue is nearly transparent without them, the white skeleton becomes visible, a process scientists call bleaching.

A bleached coral is not dead yet, but it is starving and vulnerable, and if the heat continues for too long, the coral can die while seaweed spreads across its skeleton; if the water cools down in time, however, the algae can gradually return, and the coral progressively regains its color.

In Saudi Arabia, researchers also cultivate small fragments of coral in underwater nurseries and then transplant them onto damaged reefs.

Individuals can contribute by keeping the ocean clean, protecting the fish that maintain healthy reefs, and never touching or standing on coral, since even careless contact can injure delicate polyps.

wrong.C: The coral shares the food the algae make; it does not eat the algae.
wrong.D: Polyps build their own limestone skeletons.

questions.stem: Reefs cover a tiny fraction of the ocean floor but shelter about a quarter of all ocean species. What can you conclude?
options: Losing reefs would affect a very large number of sea creatures.
Most sea creatures live far from reefs and would not be affected.
Reefs are too small to matter to the ocean.
Coral reefs contain no fish.
questions.why: Because so many species depend on such a small area, damage to reefs threatens a large share of ocean life.

wrong.B: A quarter of species depend on reefs, which is a large share.
wrong.C: The statistic shows reefs matter a great deal.
wrong.D: The article says reefs shelter many species, including fish.

questions.stem: How does the recovery of a single bleached coral differ from the recovery of a whole reef?
options: A coral needs its algae back; a reef also needs larvae and fish.
A single coral needs parrotfish, but a reef needs nothing.
Both recover instantly once the water cools.
A single coral needs new larvae, while a reef needs only cooler water.
questions.why: The article says a coral regains color when algae return, while a damaged reef recovers as larvae settle and parrotfish graze seaweed, over ten years or more.

wrong.B: Reef recovery depends on larvae and fish.
wrong.C: Reef recovery can take ten years or more.
wrong.D: This reverses the two processes.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the information about underwater nurseries in Saudi Arabia?
options: To show that people can actively help damaged reefs recover
To prove that bleaching only happens near Saudi Arabia
To explain how algae make food
To describe how parrotfish eat
questions.why: The nurseries are an example of people growing and transplanting coral to speed reef recovery.

wrong.B: The article describes bleaching as a global problem.
wrong.C: Algae and food are explained in an earlier paragraph.
wrong.D: Parrotfish are described in the recovery paragraph, not the nursery part.

HIGH.prompt: Explain why rising ocean temperatures are a serious problem for coral reefs, and describe at least two things that can help reefs recover. Use evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained how warmer water causes bleaching.
I described at least two things that help reefs recover.
I supported my ideas with evidence from the article.
